t: Number Of Rectangles That Can Form The Largest Square
o:
Every rectangle `[l, w]` hides a square of side `min(l, w)` — trim the longer side down and that is the biggest square it can yield. So the task collapses to: compute `side_i = min(l_i, w_i)` for every rectangle, find the maximum `maxLen`, and count how many rectangles achieve it.

Example 1 gives sides `[5,3,5,5]`; the largest possible side is 5 and it appears 3 times, matching the expected output. Example 2 gives sides `[2,3,3,3]` → max 3, count 3.

With at most 1000 rectangles any linear scan is instant; the only real decisions are whether to buffer the sides (two passes) or fuse max-finding and counting into one pass, and remembering that values reach 10^9 so only comparisons — never area arithmetic — should be used.
k: The largest square cuttable from [l, w] has side min(l, w) — reduce the geometry to one number per rectangle.
"Max, then count" fuses into a single pass by resetting the counter whenever a strictly larger side appears.
Sides reach 10^9, but the algorithm only compares them, so overflow is never a concern.

a.n: Approach 1: Two Passes — Compute Sides, Then Count the Max
a.i: The most transparent translation of the statement: turn each rectangle into its achievable square side, take the maximum of that list, then count occurrences. Three cheap passes over at most 1000 items.
s: Map every rectangle to side = min(l, w).
Find the maximum side across the list.
Count how many sides equal that maximum.
a.t: O(n) — constant work per rectangle across three linear passes.

a.i: Track the best side seen so far and how many rectangles achieved it while scanning once: a strictly larger side resets the counter to 1, an equal side increments it, anything smaller is ignored. One pass, O(1) memory, and it naturally handles streaming input.
s: For each rectangle compute side = min(l, w).
If side > best, set best = side and count = 1; else if side == best, increment count.

w: Either solution is interview-ready; mentioning the one-pass fusion shows attention to detail. Pitfalls: taking max(l, w) instead of min, comparing squared areas (unnecessary and overflow-prone), and mishandling the reset semantics when a new maximum appears. The constraint l_i != w_i means inputs are true rectangles, but the logic tolerates squares anyway. Follow-ups: also report the maximal side itself (trivial), handle streaming input where revisiting elements is impossible — Approach 2 already is the streaming form — or extend to counting rectangles achieving each distinct side length (use a hash map).
